The evidence points to three distinct constraints: resources becoming available on time, partners reporting their use, and services operating safely where people need them. A larger pledge total can coexist with a reporting gap and uneven access. This study follows those stages; it cannot determine a response-wide amount independently verified at facilities.
Start with the funding stages

The outbreak was declared in May 2026. WHO’s latest reviewed bulletin reports 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 deaths in the DRC as of 17 November. These surveillance counts establish the scale of the emergency; they do not identify the effect of any financing decision. [07]

A pledge is an announced contribution. A disbursement records a payment to a recipient, often an implementing organization. Expenditure records use of resources. Frontline delivery needs a dated receipt, payroll confirmation or service record at the delivery point. An in-kind donation requires its own valuation, dispatch and acceptance records. Repeated transfers of the same funds must retain one identifier.

The September pledge table’s 40 entries sum to $2,997.07m, close to its printed $2.997bn total. The headline uses approximately $2.9bn. The study retains these labels rather than turning their rounding difference into a cash discrepancy. [01]
October: a measurable reporting gap

Africa CDC clarified that the $962m had been paid directly to implementing partners. The declarations available at the meeting covered $220m: $120m reported spent and $100m available. The arithmetic leaves $742m outside that reporting view. These are agency-reported aggregates, not audited facility receipts. [03]

blocks.text: October: a measurable reporting gap

By 15 November, the reported visibility amount was $820m. That is a later accounting view containing spending and balances. The $1.2bn comparator includes transfers in process. Dividing the two would create a mixed-basis ratio; it would not measure the share of settled cash reaching patients. [04]
What frontline evidence establishes

The joint 15 November operational statement reports delayed payments to responders and significant expansion of services. It also describes insecurity interrupting operations. These findings support several possible bottlenecks rather than a single explanation for continued transmission. [08]

A useful donor example is the World Bank’s $426.6m package: its release explicitly includes current and planned financing. The included $80m and $13m tranches are not additional amounts to sum again. Its reported detection-time improvement, from 10 days to one or two days, remains a donor-reported outcome without a transaction-level causal attribution. [11]

This location measure is a warning about timely access, not an estimate of avoidable deaths. Treatment selection, disease severity, detection and insecurity can all affect who appears in each group. A cost-per-life-saved calculation would require additional clinical and counterfactual evidence.
An aggregate pledge does not resolve every service gap
UNICEF’s 6 October snapshot put its DRC requirement at $113.4m and mobilized resources at $40.1m. That leaves $73.3m, or 64.6%, in that historical programme scope. [09]
UNICEF DRC financing snapshot · 6 October · US$ million
UNICEF DRC financing snapshot · 6 October · US$ million

A separate 24 November UNICEF statement reports a 76% funding gap for protection activities for children and women. Its dollar denominator is not supplied. The two snapshots illustrate allocation pressure; they cannot be combined or treated as a time series. [10]
The revised plan changes the financing question

The new $1.576bn estimate covers countries and partners. The DRC government requirement of approximately $1.231bn is within the plan’s scope. A new funding gap cannot be calculated by subtracting old visibility or pledge totals: earlier spending, remaining balances, earmarks, period and coverage must first be reconciled. [06]

The financing test is therefore forward-looking: what unspent, usable resources are available for the new phase, in which places and for which activities? Published plans supply a requirement. Recipient records must establish the usable balance.

The incremental research task is a reconciliation across these records. A separate dashboard would add little unless it demonstrably improves completeness, verification time or decisions. No new product is proposed. National coordination can require financial information without assuming that every grant must pass through one government account. [12]

These windows are proposed research milestones. Keep care continuous during checks, protect payroll and patient identifiers, aggregate sensitive findings, and avoid publishing exact sensitive facility locations. Verification should fit existing coordination and reporting routines.
Method and limits

This is a document-based diagnostic as of 25 November 2026. Primary agency statements, the official plan and donor releases anchor the evidence; the November financial update is attributed through ACP. Joint statements and their reposts count as one source. Calculations use the published figures with their original scopes and dates.

The October clarification takes precedence over rounded retellings using $200m or $260m. Dynamic HealthCheck snapshots differed during retrieval, and its CSV could not be downloaded; its aggregate totals are excluded from the calculations. The official financial dashboard and HEAT are documented in the plan, but live underlying records were not retrieved. No banks, payroll systems, patients or facility records were accessed.

Source-reported amounts are distinguished from modelled requirements and original arithmetic. There is no audited response-wide frontline total, finding of diversion, causal mortality estimate or investment-return claim. The conclusion remains conditional on fuller records: financing, reporting and safe operational access all require separate measurement.
